parts.partTitle: Why String Is Immutable & Compact Strings

beats.headline: Strings consume 40% of your heap.
beats.subline: Java string immutability isn't syntactic sugar—it powers caching, security, and memory pooling.
beats.narration: In busy enterprise microservices, string objects swallow up to 40 percent of total heap space. Java enforces strict string immutability to guarantee memory safety, cached hash codes, and thread-safe reference sharing.

beats.title: The Hidden Power of Immutability

top.label: If String Were Mutable
points: HashMap keys drift and break bucket lookups

bottom.label: Java Final String
points: Safe sharing across threads without locks
Hash code cached permanently after first check

beats.narration: If strings were mutable, a separate thread could alter a validated path before execution. Java prevents this by marking string final, caching its hash code, and allowing safe sharing across threads.

beats.title: Compact Strings Layout (Java 9+ JEP 254)
beats.subtitle: Replacing 2-byte char arrays with adaptive byte arrays

nodes.label: String Object Header
nodes.detail: 12-16 byte object overhead + cached int hash

nodes.label: Coder Field (1 Byte)
nodes.detail: 0 for LATIN1 (1 byte/char), 1 for UTF16 (2 bytes/char)

nodes.label: Backing byte[] Array
nodes.detail: Stores Latin-1 ASCII text at 1 byte per character

nodes.label: Memory Savings
nodes.detail: Cuts memory footprint by 50% for English & JSON keys

beats.narration: Before Java 9, strings used UTF-16 char arrays taking two bytes per character. Compact Strings replaced char array with a byte array and a coder flag, cutting heap memory usage by half for Latin-1 text.

beats.title: Latin-1 vs. UTF-16 Encoding in Action

steps.explanation: Fits in ISO-8859-1, allocating exactly one byte per character on heap.
Emoji forces entire backing array to expand to 2 bytes per character.

beats.narration: When text contains only Latin-1 characters, Java sets coder to zero, taking one byte per char. Adding an emoji forces coder to one, expanding the backing byte array to two bytes per character.

beats.title: Immutability & Compact Strings Locked In
takeaways: Immutability enables safe sharing & cached hash codes
Compact Strings save 50% heap for Latin-1 text
coder flag switches dynamically between LATIN1 and UTF16

parts.partTitle: The String Constant Pool & Memory Deduplication

beats.headline: literal1 == dynamicString returns false.
beats.subline: String literals share pool references, but runtime strings create separate heap objects.
beats.narration: Comparing strings with double equals works fine in local tests, then fails in production. Let's inspect how the String Constant Pool handles literals versus dynamic heap objects.

beats.title: String Constant Pool (StringTable) Architecture
beats.subtitle: Native hash table inside Java Heap (moved out of PermGen in Java 7)

nodes.label: Thread Stack References
nodes.detail: s1 and s2 point to pool, s3 points to distinct heap string

nodes.label: Heap Memory Objects
nodes.detail: new String() creates separate unpooled heap instances

nodes.label: Garbage Collector
nodes.detail: Reclaims unused pooled strings automatically since Java 7

beats.narration: String literals reside in the String Constant Pool, a native hash table inside the Java heap. Variables holding identical literals share the same object, while new String calls allocate unnecessary heap duplicates.

beats.title: Reference Equality vs. Content Equality

top.label: Double Equals Check (==)
points: Fails when dynamic text comes from DB or JSON

bottom.label: .equals() Value Check
points: Compares actual character sequences byte by byte
Placing literal on left avoids NullPointerException

beats.narration: Double equals checks if two references share the exact same memory address. Always use equals to compare characters, and put literals on the left to prevent null pointer exceptions automatically.

beats.title: Manual intern() vs. G1GC Deduplication
beats.caption: Avoid native StringTable lock contention under load

lines.text: # 1. Manual interning paid native lookup & locking costs
Warning: High cardinality strings fill native StringTable
# 2. Modern JDK solution: Enable G1GC String Deduplication
GC repoints identical byte arrays to 1 shared array in background

beats.narration: Calling intern manually forces native table lookups that slow down high-concurrency apps. Instead, enable G1GC String Deduplication to let garbage collection merge identical backing byte arrays transparently.

beats.title: Pool Mechanics Mastered
takeaways: Compile-time constant strings fold into pool automatically

beats.headline: Using + in a loop creates an O(n²) garbage avalanche.
beats.subline: Immutable strings force every loop iteration to copy all accumulated characters into new arrays.
beats.narration: Appending strings with the plus operator inside a loop is an enterprise memory disaster. Every single iteration copies all previously accumulated characters into a brand new heap array.

beats.title: Loop Appending vs. Single Expression Concatenation

top.label: Loop String Appending (+)
points: Copies billions of bytes, melting CPU & GC

bottom.label: Single Expression (+)
bottom.code:
String log = "User " + id + " logged in at " + time;
// Uses StringConcatFactory.makeConcatWithConstants
points: Computes exact total length upfront in 1 pass
Allocates a single byte array with zero buffer resizes

beats.narration: Outside loops, single expression concatenation uses invokedynamic and StringConcatFactory to compute length upfront. Inside loops, plus causes quadratic character copying and floods the heap with garbage.

beats.title: Linear Performance with Pre-Sized StringBuilder

steps.explanation: Pass estimated capacity upfront so backing byte array never resizes.
Writes directly into internal buffer without creating intermediate strings.

beats.narration: Using StringBuilder in loops converts quadratic allocations into linear time. Pre-sizing capacity upfront prevents internal array growth overhead, keeping string construction fast and lean.

beats.title: Bytecode Inspection with javap -c
beats.caption: See invokedynamic vs StringBuilder in bytecode

lines.text: # Loop '+' emits repetitive StringBuilder allocations inside loop body:

beats.narration: Disassembling bytecode with javap reveals that single line concatenation emits a fast invokedynamic instruction. But loop concatenation compiles into repeated builder instantiations inside the loop.

beats.title: Concatenation Mastered
takeaways: Never append strings with + inside loops
Single expression + uses invokedynamic in Java 9+
Pre-size StringBuilder buffers for linear O(n) runtime

beats.headline: Stop using StringBuffer in modern Java.
beats.subline: Method-level synchronization adds monitor lock overhead without making multi-step calls atomic.
beats.narration: Synchronizing individual append calls does not make multithreaded string operations atomic. Legacy StringBuffer only adds lock acquisition overhead without offering true thread safety.

beats.title: StringBuffer vs. StringBuilder vs. String.join

top.label: StringBuffer (Java 1.0 Legacy)
points: Locks monitor even when object is local to one thread

bottom.label: StringBuilder & String.join
points: Zero synchronization overhead on single-threaded ops
StringJoiner handles delimiters cleanly without loop logic

beats.narration: StringBuffer synchronizes every method call individually, creating unnecessary lock contention. Use unsynchronized StringBuilder for local code, or String dot join for clean delimited output.

beats.title: Buffer Capacity Growth & UTF-16 Inflation

steps.explanation: Exceeding capacity allocates a new array sized (oldCapacity * 2) + 2.
Single multi-byte Unicode char doubles byte array size for all characters.

beats.narration: StringBuilder starts with a default capacity of 16 characters. When exceeded, it resizes using double old capacity plus two, and adding a Unicode character inflates the whole array to UTF-16.

beats.title: StringBuilder Internal Lifecycle
beats.subtitle: Buffer allocation, growth, coder inflation, and final materialization

nodes.label: UTF16 Coder Inflation
nodes.detail: Inflates backing array from LATIN1 to UTF16 if emoji appended

nodes.label: toString() Call
nodes.detail: Materializes final immutable String instance on heap

beats.narration: Under the hood, StringBuilder manages a resizable byte array. It grows using double plus two expansion, inflates to UTF-16 when needed, and materializes into an immutable String when toString is called.

beats.title: Chapter Complete! Run the Lab
takeaways: Use StringBuilder over legacy synchronized StringBuffer
Pre-size builder capacity to avoid double-plus-two array copies
Use String.join or StringJoiner for clean delimited output
